headlines.html: Galaxia unveils OSPREY to receive and process other satellites’ data in orbit: With support from Canada’s Department of National Defence, the company is developing a demonstration satellite combining data relay with onboard computing. — (Galaxia)

Ubotica reports satellite AI autonomously scheduled and executed follow-up imaging: After detecting a ship, the satellite imaged the same location again two days later without ground commands. — (Ubotica)

2026-11-06.summary_html:
① Galaxia (11/4) — (2026-11-04) Supported by the Canadian Department of National Defence’s IDEaS program, OSPREY will test receiving data from existing satellites in orbit and either processing it onboard or forwarding it to other low Earth orbit communications networks. The spacecraft will integrate computing, security and communications capabilities on the company’s Halifax Class platform. No launch date or processing performance figures have been disclosed. The project remains in development and is not a commercial service.

② Ubotica (11/4) — (2026-11-04) According to the company, AI aboard CogniSAT-6 detected a cruise ship in the Pacific Ocean in early October, calculated the next imaging opportunity and imaged the same location again two days later without ground commands. The test was conducted on a 6U satellite built and operated by Open Cosmos. It demonstrated autonomous onboard computing on a single satellite, rather than a computing network operating across multiple satellites. Both developments highlight the potential of orbital computing to reduce the volume of data sent to the ground and shorten response times. Galaxia is developing a system to handle processing tasks for other satellites, while Ubotica has linked observation results directly to a satellite’s next action. Together, the announcements suggest that scaling these capabilities into orbital data centers will require validation of reliable intersatellite links, computing resource allocation and actual processing performance.

headlines.html: Lonestar and Coral Gables launch space-based data backup pilot: The 12-month program will test storage of municipal recovery data and historical records, with the storage system scheduled to launch in April 2027. — (Lonestar)

2026-11-05.summary_html:
① Lonestar (11/2) — (2026-11-02) The U.S. city of Coral Gables is joining StarVault as a founding city partner. The 12-month pilot will supplement existing backups with space-based storage to protect municipal recovery data, security keys and historical records. The city will retain access to its data and is preparing materials ahead of the April 2027 launch. No operational results from the space-based backup system have been announced. Demand for orbital data centers is emerging not only for large-scale AI computing but also for disaster recovery storage. This pilot offers a test of the value of physically remote storage while the city maintains its existing backups. Beyond the launch itself, the key measures will be whether data can be successfully recovered, how long recovery takes and how much the service costs to operate.

headlines.html: South Korea plans 100 kg-class orbital data center demonstration aboard Nuri in 2028: The mission would test domestically developed AI chips, power systems and thermal management technologies, with approximately ₩14 billion in funding still to be secured. — (Newsis·Financial News)

KT SAT discloses international registration filing for 7,000 satellites for orbital AI data centers: The company said it submitted the filing to the ITU early this year and coordination is underway; the filing does not constitute approval or a confirmed launch plan. — (Edaily)

Beijing announces cloud platform linking computing resources on some 40 satellites with ground infrastructure: Authorities announced the implementation of core functions and integrated resource management for the platform unveiled on October 30. — (Beijing Municipal Science and Technology Commission·Beijing economic and information technology authorities)

2026-11-04.summary_html:
① K-Moonshot·Korea Aerospace Research Institute (Newsis·Financial News, 11/2) — (2026-11-02) Plans presented at a National Assembly forum call for a single 100 kg-class demonstration satellite to fly on Nuri’s seventh launch in November 2028. The mission would test domestically developed AI chips, power systems and thermal management technologies, paving the way for a larger-scale system in 2034. The initial demonstration requires approximately ₩14 billion, with funding yet to be secured.

② KT SAT (Edaily, 11/3) — (2026-11-03) CEO Choi Kyung-il said at the previous day’s forum that the company had submitted an international frequency and orbital registration filing to the ITU early this year for 7,000 satellites intended for orbital AI data centers. The filing is in the coordination phase and does not constitute deployment approval. He also proposed that the government serve as an anchor customer to support commercial infrastructure targeted for 2035.

③ Beijing Space Computing Innovation Center (Beijing Municipal Science and Technology Commission, 11/3) — (2026-11-03) The platform unveiled on October 30 is described as providing integrated management of computing resources on some 40 satellites and ground-based CPUs, GPUs and NPUs. It also connects to Baidu Cloud’s model and data interfaces. The platform pools existing resources; the announcement does not mean that some 40 new satellites have been launched. No measured throughput figures were provided. Taken together, these announcements show that competition in orbital data centers requires space qualification of components, frequency and orbital coordination, and the operational capability to combine distributed computing resources into services. South Korea’s demonstration roadmap and private-sector commercialization proposals still need to bring funding, customers and operators together. The number of resources connected to China’s platform likewise does not establish its commercial performance. Actual workload throughput and reliable service delivery will be the next benchmarks to assess.

headlines.html: Starcloud and Quindar partner on orbital data center operations: The companies are developing software to manage missions aboard satellites even when ground connectivity is lost. — (Quindar)
Satlyt tests workload allocation in orbit: — (TechCrunch)

2026-11-02.summary_html:
① Starcloud and Quindar (Quindar, 10/28) — (2026-10-28) The companies plan to deploy Quindar’s mission management platform aboard Starcloud satellites. They will test operational continuity between ground and orbital clouds, onboard data processing, and real-time decision-making based on satellite health. The work will use Starcloud-1 and Starcloud-2; measured uptime figures and a service launch date have not been disclosed.

② Satlyt (TechCrunch, 10/30) — (2026-10-30) Satlyt tested workload allocation across a virtual network running on a single computer in orbit. Connectivity between multiple physical computers has yet to be validated. The company’s vision for software collaboration between satellites is also outlined on its [official website](https://satlyt.ai/). This briefing’s assessment is that progress should be evaluated by distinguishing between putting hardware in orbit and operating multiple systems together. These developments suggest that competition in orbital data centers is expanding from computing hardware to operational software. In this briefing’s analysis, decisions about where to assign workloads and how to respond to failures when communications are unreliable will determine service reliability. The next milestone is whether partnerships and limited tests can translate into sustained commercial operations.
